title: India and the US Say a Trade Deal Is Days Away. Here's What's Actually Holding It Up.
excerpt: Greer flew to Delhi, Goyal flew to London, and both sides called it 'very, very close.' But the Supreme Court ruling, Section 301, and a July 24 deadline are making the final stretch harder than the first mile.
body:
For the first time in months, both sides are using the same word. "Very close," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said in London last week. "Very, very close," echoed Bethany Poulos Morrison, the U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary for South and Central Asian Affairs, at a separate event days later. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, fresh off a two-day visit to New Delhi, told reporters the relationship was heading "to a higher and higher level with every passing week."

The question is whether the mood matches the math.

What Was Agreed, and What Broke

The story begins in February 2026, when Modi and Trump announced an initial understanding: 18 per cent tariffs on Indian goods coming into the U.S. — significantly lower than the rates facing Bangladesh (37 per cent) or Vietnam (46 per cent). In exchange, India would lower trade barriers and buy more American goods. It looked like a genuine breakthrough.

Then the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated Trump's sweeping global tariffs, throwing the legal framework for any bilateral deal into uncertainty. Washington's trade negotiators were suddenly without the instrument they had been using — and New Delhi was left waiting for clarity on what "tools and legal backing" the Americans would deploy instead.

On top of that, the USTR launched a Section 301 investigation into alleged overcapacity and forced labour in India and several other countries. The probe infuriated New Delhi, which sees it as both factually wrong and strategically counterproductive at a moment when both sides are supposed to be building trust.

What Greer Came to Discuss

Greer arrived in New Delhi on June 22 for two days of talks with Goyal, accompanied by U.S. Ambassador Sergio Gor and a full trade delegation. Their agenda was threefold: advance the interim deal, align on a pathway to a broader Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA), and address the legal vacuum left by the Supreme Court ruling.

The joint statement after the talks was diplomatic but specific. Both sides noted "substantial progress" and discussed "pathways to conclude an interim agreement." Greer called it "an important milestone toward a comprehensive BTA." Goyal, speaking in London the next day, said: "The day that happens — when Washington finds the appropriate legal backing — the deal is on."

India's demand is clear: a tariff rate that gives it a competitive edge over ASEAN peers, not just parity. "We are trying to work out with the U.S. how they will ensure that we will get a comparative advantage, so that our exporters can benefit," Goyal said before the meetings began.

The July 24 Clock

The pressure point is a calendar date. Washington's temporary 10 per cent tariff on trading partners — the placeholder rate imposed while deals are being negotiated — expires on July 24. If no agreement is in place by then, Indian goods could face sharply higher duties. Goyal has said he would be "happy" if a deal is finalised before that deadline. "The faster, the better."

India also wants assurances that Washington will not levy new tariffs after a deal is signed — a concern driven by the unpredictability of the current U.S. administration's trade posture.

The Damage So Far

The urgency is not abstract. According to a report by the Global Trade Research Initiative, Indian exports to the United States have already plunged 37.5 per cent over four months — from $8.8 billion in May 2025 to $5.5 billion by September, when the 50 per cent tariff fully took effect. Textiles, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, and chemicals have been hit hardest.

The broader bilateral trade target — "Mission 500," an ambition to hit $500 billion in two-way trade by 2030 — looks increasingly disconnected from reality. Even Morrison, while promoting the target, acknowledged that achieving it would require "a real sense of urgency."

What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora in the U.S., the deal has implications beyond macro-economics. Lower tariffs would make Indian goods cheaper on American shelves — from textiles to spices to pharmaceuticals. A deal would also ease the broader diplomatic temperature between Washington and New Delhi at a time when visa policy, consular relations, and the treatment of Indian students have all become friction points.

More immediately, a failed negotiation could trigger retaliatory measures from both sides, disrupting the business environment for the thousands of Indian-American entrepreneurs who trade across the corridor.

The next few weeks will determine whether "very, very close" becomes a signed agreement or a diplomatic epitaph.

*Sources: Reuters, Global Trade Research Initiative, U.S. Trade Representative, India Ministry of Commerce*
